Multistage Amplifiers: Cascades, Darlington, Cascode, Direct Coupling and Current Mirrors

Why this matters in the exam: Multistage circuits sit on top of everything in E6/E7. A cascade question is really two single-stage questions plus one loading step, so it is a cheap way for an examiner to test the whole small-signal method. Practice Test Q8 (6 of 50 marks) is a two-BJT DC question, and WS6 Q12–Q19 are all two-transistor circuits. WS9 Q9 repeats the cascade idea with JFETs, so the loading method you learn here carries over to the FET half of the final. Expect one 6–10 mark question that chains a DC bias, a loaded first-stage gain and an overall gain.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The one rule of cascades

Stage 2’s input impedance is stage 1’s load. Once you have that, the overall gain is just the product of the loaded stage gains:

where is computed with in parallel with stage 1’s collector resistor, with (or for the last stage), and so on. The Week 5 slide “Cascaded Systems” also gives the total current gain . The sign depends on the direction you define , so use the convention your question gives.

RC coupling (Week 5 slide 62): a coupling capacitor joins stage 1’s collector to stage 2’s base. It blocks DC, so each stage is biased on its own with the usual voltage-divider analysis. At signal frequency is a short.

1.5 Cascode (slides 75–79, WS6 Q15)

Q1 is a CE stage whose collector feeds Q2’s emitter. Q2 is common-base, with its base held at an AC ground by a capacitor. A three-resistor divider (top), , (bottom) sets both base voltages:

AC: Q1’s load is , which is tiny, so . Q2 (CB) gives . Overall , the same as a single CE stage.

Why it helps: the same current flows through both transistors, so the gain is unchanged. But Q1 has a voltage gain of only about , so its collector–base capacitance is barely multiplied (the Miller effect, Week 10). The result is the same gain over a much wider bandwidth, plus a high output impedance. Trap: writing “the cascode has higher gain than a CE stage”. At the same and , it does not.

1.6 Direct-coupled stages (slides 84–88, WS6 Q16)

There is no coupling capacitor, so stage 1’s DC collector voltage is stage 2’s DC base voltage. Work forwards: bias stage 1 (Thévenin), find , then set , , and so on. The slides and WS6 solution take , which ignores Q2’s base current flowing out of . This is fine when is large. If is not small compared with , say so (see Traps). Advantages: good low-frequency response and fewer components. Disadvantage: any DC drift in stage 1 is amplified by stage 2.

1.7 Current mirror (slides 89–90, WS6 Q18–Q19)

Q1 is diode-connected (its collector is tied to its base). Q2 is identical and shares the same , so it carries the same current.

1.8 Push-pull / complementary pairs (WS6 Q14, briefly)

The workshop intro mentions a “simple push-pull topology” for DC analysis. The Week 5 slides do not cover push-pull output stages. For exam purposes this means npn–pnp pairs (WS6 Q14, Practice Test Q8). An npn emitter sits 0.7 V below its base. A pnp emitter sits 0.7 V above its base. With , the base currents are zero, so a base node is set only by the resistor network around it.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using no-load gains for every stage and multiplying. Stage 1 must be loaded by . In the lecture example this mistake gives instead of , an error of more than 3×.
  • Wrong formula. For an unbypassed stage 2 it is , not . This is exactly the difference between Prac 4 Figure 1 (3.52 kΩ) and Figure 3 (941 Ω).
  • Forgetting in . The bias divider of stage 2 loads stage 1 as much as the transistor does.
  • Sign and phase. Each CE stage inverts. Two CE stages give a positive gain. CB and EF stages do not invert. Write the sign on every stage gain.
  • Including in , or in . and belong to the amplifier. and only appear in the dividers.
  • Not checking the output against the supply. A gain of 463 with a 30 mV input demands 13.9 V, which clips (Prac 4 Step 7 showed the same thing with a gain of about 36,000).
  • Darlington with one . Two junctions are in series (1.4 V, or 1.6 V if the datasheet value is given). For a current mirror, remember the factor is , because both base currents come out of .
  • pnp direction. A pnp emitter sits 0.7 V above its base. The official WS6 Q14 solution makes exactly this slip; see §5.

Reading the figure: V and V rails. Node A is ’s base, tied to ground through 10 kΩ. is npn: collector C goes through 10 kΩ to +20 V, and emitter B goes through 9.3 kΩ to −10 V. is pnp: its base is at node C, emitter D goes through 9.3 kΩ to +20 V, and collector E goes through 10 kΩ to −10 V.

Where the official solution goes wrong: it writes V, which treats the emitter as 0.7 V above ground instead of above the base (node C = 10 V). It then gets mA and V, and concludes that is saturated. That conclusion is wrong. does not disconnect the base from node C; it only means no current flows in that wire. The symmetric resistor values (10 k / 9.3 k on both sides) are a strong hint that the designer intended 1 mA in each transistor and both active.

Lecture Wk5 ex (both bypassed, b=200, re=6.34): Av1=-104, Av2=-347, AvT=36.1e3; RL=4.7k -> 24.6e3
Prac4 Fig1 (stage 2 UNBYPASSED): Zi2=3.52k, Av1=-212, Av2=-2.19 -> 463; RL=4.7k -> 316; Zi1=941, Zo2=2.2k
Darlington: bD=b1*b2, VBE=2 drops (1.4 V; 1.6 V Boylestad)
  IB=(VCC-VBE)/(RB+bD*RE), Zi=RB||bD*RE, Ai~bD*RB/(RB+bD*RE), Av~1
Feedback pair: IB1=(VCC-VEB1)/(RB+b1*b2*RC), one VBE drop
Cascode: VB1=R3/(R1+R2+R3)*VCC, VB2=(R2+R3)/(R1+R2+R3)*VCC, IE=(VB1-0.7)/RE same both
  VC1=VB2-0.7, Av1=-1, Av2=+RC/re, Av~-RC/re; benefit = bandwidth (low Miller), not gain
Direct-coupled: VB2 = VC1 = VCC - IC1*RC1 (check IB2 << IC1, else KCL at node)
Mirror: IREF=(VCC - VB1)/R, VB1 = emitter rail + 0.7;  Io = IREF/(1+2/b) -> IREF
  Design: R = (VCC - VB1)/[Io(1+2/b)]; keep output BJT active (VCE>=0.2)
npn: VE = VB - 0.7     pnp: VE = VB + 0.7     beta = inf -> IB = 0
